## Common Collocations
- **aprobar una ley** — to pass a law; uses **aprobar**, not **pasar**
- **violar los derechos** — to violate rights; **violar** also means "to rape" — context critical
- **convocar elecciones** — to call elections; not **llamar elecciones**
- **hacer campaña** — to campaign; verbal form uses **hacer**
- **tomar el poder** — to seize power; not **agarrar** or **coger**
- **dar un discurso** — to give a speech; not **hacer un discurso**
- **estar a favor de / en contra de** — to be for / against; always with **estar**, never **ser**
- **sin embargo** — however; key D-06 connector, very frequent in political discussion

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **la política** vs **politics/policy**: One word covers both. "Foreign policy" = **la política exterior**. "Politics is complicated" = **La política es complicada**. Context is the only disambiguator.
- **la campaña** vs **campaign**: Also means "countryside" (**la campaña** in Argentina/Uruguay = rural area). In most countries, **el campo** is "countryside."
- **exigir** vs **demand**: **Exigir** is "to demand" (insist on). **Demandar** means "to sue" in legal contexts. English speakers default to **demandar** incorrectly.
- **el partido** vs **party**: Also means "game/match" (**un partido de futbol**). A social party is **una fiesta**.
- **la manifestación** vs **manifestation**: Primary meaning is "protest/demonstration" (public rally). The English sense of "manifestation" is secondary.

## Dialect Variations
- **el congreso** vs **la asamblea** vs **el parlamento**: Varies by country. Mexico: **el Congreso**. Spain: **el Parlamento** and **las Cortes**. Venezuela: **la Asamblea Nacional**.
- **la policía** (institution) vs **el/la policía** (individual officer): Universal, but informal terms vary — **la placa** (Colombia), **la tira** (Mexico slang), **los pacos** (Chile).
- **el barrio** vs **la colonia**: Mexico uses **colonia** for neighborhood. Most other countries use **barrio**.
- **votar** pronunciation: In regions with b/v merger (most of Latin America), sounds identical to **botar** (to throw away). Context disambiguates.

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Political discussion norms**: Political topics are common in casual conversation across Latin America and Spain — less taboo than in some English-speaking cultures. Expect direct opinions and passionate debate.
- **Passive constructions in news**: Political journalism relies heavily on passive **se** and **ser** + past participle (D-04). Reading news headlines is excellent practice: **Se aprobó la ley**, **Fue elegido el nuevo presidente**.
- **Nuanced connectors in editorials**: Newspaper opinion columns are dense with D-06 connectors: **sin embargo**, **no obstante**, **a pesar de que**, **por lo tanto**. Use editorials as reading practice for both vocabulary and grammar.
- **Formality in political speech**: Politicians use **usted** and formal register universally, even when addressing supporters. This makes political speeches good listening practice for formal register.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **gobierno** — four syllables: go-BIER-no. English speakers tend to add a syllable: go-bi-ER-no.
- **democracia** — stress on third syllable: de-mo-CRA-cia. Not de-MO-cra-cia.
- **inmigración** — stress on final syllable: in-mi-gra-CIÓN. Written accent required.
- **igualdad** — stress on final syllable: i-gual-DAD. No written accent (stress on final syllable ending in -d is regular).
- **ciudadano** — four syllables: ciu-da-DA-no. The **ciu** is one syllable (diphthong).
